subject: Science
theme: Plant structure and function - root hair physiology and transplant stress
question_short_text: Why transplanted seedlings fail to grow - role of root hairs
text: Many transplanted seedlings do not grow because?
options: The new soil does not contain favourable minerals
Most of the root hairs grip the new soil too hard
Most of the root hairs are lost during transplantation
answerText: (c) Most of the root hairs are lost during transplantation
explanation: Root hairs are the primary absorptive organs of the plant root system. During transplantation, these delicate microscopic structures are mechanically damaged or torn away from the soil matrix, causing significant loss. Without adequate root hairs, the seedling cannot absorb sufficient water and nutrients from the new soil, leading to stunted growth or failure to establish.

research.summary: The correct answer targets a physiological limitation rather than a soil or leaf issue. Root hairs are highly specialized epidermal cell extensions whose primary function is water and mineral nutrient absorption—in roots, most water absorption occurs through root hairs. These structures increase the absorptive surface area dramatically: a single root hair is only 80–1,500 micrometers in length, yet their collective presence can expand root surface area by up to 180% in some species. The trap in this question lies in assuming that transplantation merely shifts the seedling to a new location. In reality, the mechanical disturbance of transplanting—pulling the seedling from nursery soil and replanting into new soil—physically severs or dislodges the delicate root hairs that were embedded in the original soil matrix. This causes an acute reduction in absorptive capacity at precisely the moment when the seedling is establishing in an unfamiliar soil environment. Option (a) is wrong because transplanted seedlings are usually moved to prepared soil of adequate fertility; mineral deficiency alone would not explain widespread failure. Option (b) misunderstands root hair function—they do not 'grip' soil but rather absorb from it passively. Option (d), while leaf damage can reduce photosynthesis, is less critical to initial establishment than root function. The key insight is that transplant shock is fundamentally a water and nutrient absorption crisis, not a structural damage crisis or a soil quality crisis. New root hairs regenerate within days to weeks after transplantation, which is why survival depends on maintaining soil moisture and temperature during this recovery window.
facts: Root hairs form only in the zone of maturation (differentiation zone) of the root and are not found in the zone of elongation, because older hairs are sheared off as the root elongates through soil.

Transplant-induced wilting occurs specifically because the loss of root hairs severely compromises water uptake capacity, not because the plant is physically damaged elsewhere; repotting can result in root hair cells being pulled off to a significant extent.
